correctness.rationale: Independently substituting the affine unit-sphere parameterization gives the strictly concave distance quadratic with vertex t_c=a(m−c)/(b²−a²). In the pole branch, −r<δ<r implies a>0 and a+δ>0, a<r, and b²−a²=3a(a+δ). The small ball has t_s=−1/3 and maximum r² from 16a²+16aδ+3δ²=3r². The larger ball has F_0(1)=R² and vertex at least 1 exactly when R−δ≥sqrt(δ²+3r²); the positive side permits squaring to give s≤s_c. Also s_c≥R+r iff R≥3r, and s_c>R−r for R>r. In the two-latitude branch, putting u²=T and v=−1/(3u) gives R²=B+Ju², r²=B+Jv², and s=J(u−v)/sqrt(B+J). The denominator factors in the squared equation are positive on R/(3r)<T≤1; the ratio (3T+1)/(3T−1) decreases and the bracket increases. The endpoint squared separations are (R+r)² and s_c², proving unique solvability. The distance maxima then occur at u,v, tending to 1,−1/3 at the transition. The equal-radius candidate has maximum squared distance a²+2as/sqrt(3)+s²/4=R² and latitudes ±1/sqrt(3). In each case weights −v/(u−v),u/(u−v) give mean zero and axial variance −uv=1/3, hence both transverse variances are 1/3 as well. John's criterion proves unrestricted unique maximality, including at the degenerate pole and at the transition, so the branch limits coincide. This is an analytic check, not a sample-to-continuum inference from the supplied checker.
